parole.significato: used with a stem to form a feminine singular noun, usually a deverbal
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -am, from Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ (forms action nouns).

parole.significato: -able (that can be …ed; that is worthy to be …ed)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ābilis. See also -évole.

parole.significato: used to create female collective nouns, often pejorative
parole.testo: From Latin -ālia, the neuter plural of -ālis.

parole.significato: added to nouns to form adjectives, often specifically relational adjectives; -al
parole.testo: From Latin -ālis.

parole.significato: the infinitive ending of most regular verbs; also, a productive suffix forming new verbs from nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āre.

parole.significato: suffix forming adjectives, often specifically relational adjectives, from nouns
parole.testo: From Latin -āris.

parole.significato: -ary; added to nouns to create relational adjective forms and show relation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ārius. Compare the inherited doublet -aio.

parole.significato: used to form verbal nouns, derived from regular -are verbs, expressing an instance of the action expressed by the verb;…
parole.testo: Nominalization of the past participle form of Etymology 1.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the past participle of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātus (second declension), from Proto-Italic *-ātos. The chemistry nouns originated as substantivized perfect passive participles from first conjugation Latin verbs; e.g. the Latin adjective acētātus in the 18th-century Latin phrase plumbum acētātum (“lead acetate”, literally “a
Inherited from Latin -ātus (fourth declension), from Proto-Italic *-tus.

parole.significato: suffix used to form noun diminutives from nouns (including proper nouns) and sometimes adjectives and verbs, often with…
parole.testo: From Latin -ellus.

parole.significato: stem, to form the infinitive of some Italian verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēre (second conjugation).

parole.significato: suffix used to form melioratives, diminutives, and hypocoristics
parole.testo: From Late Latin -ittus.

parole.significato: added to adjectives to form abstract nouns; -ity; -ness
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -itia, whence also Italian -izia, a borrowed doublet. Cognate with Sicilian -izza.

parole.significato: derives abstract nouns denoting a state or condition from adjectives or nouns
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -ία (-ía).

parole.significato: -ible (that can be …ed; that is worthy to be …ed)
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from Latin -ibilis. Compare the inherited doublet -évole.
Derived from Latin -icus.
From Latin -idus.

parole.significato: inflectional suffix used to form diminutives of feminine nouns
parole.testo: From Latin -īna.
From Latin -īnus. Compare English -ine.

parole.significato: used with some -ire verbs to make the present stem
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēscere.

parole.significato: added to adjectives to form absolute superlatives
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -issimus. Compare Spanish -ísimo and Portuguese -íssimo which are partly based on the Italian forms.

parole.significato: Attaches to an adjective in the feminine singular to form the corresponding adverb.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mente.

parole.significato: forms nouns that represent the action of a related verb
parole.testo: From Latin -mentum.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form a masculine singular noun, usually a deverbal
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -um, from Proto-Indo-European *-os (creates action nouns from verbs).

parole.significato: used to form a diminutive of a masculine noun, indicating small size or youth
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -olus.

parole.significato: denotes small size or petty nature
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ulus. Compare adjectives piccolo and ridicolo.
From Latin -ōsus.

parole.significato: added to verbs to form masculine nouns and adjectives from verbs with the sense of "person or thing connected or involv…
parole.testo: From Latin -tōrem, from Proto-Italic *-tōr, from Proto-Indo-European *-tōr < *-tor-s. Cognate to French -eur, -teur, Spanish -dor, Sicilian -turi.
From Vulgar Latin -uc(c)ulus, -(uc)cula, from -(uc)culum, from the Latin diminutive suffix -culus (feminine -cula, neuter -culum). Compare also Sicilian -uzzu, Romanian -uț.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the past participle of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -ūtus.

parole.significato: used to form nouns relating to the action of specified verbs; -ation; -tion
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -tiōnem, as a learned form. The original inherited form of the suffix, -zone and -zzone or in some cases -gione, is today less common but found in words such as ragione, stagione, cagione, canzone, punzone, acquazzone, tizzone, etc.
From Latin ad. In a few phrases, a stems from Latin ā, ab.
Inherited from Latin ad-.
Borrowed from Latin agnus, from Proto-Italic *agʷnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷnós. Cognate with Albanian enjë, Czech jehně, Greek αμνός (amnós), Irish uan.
From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Doublet of Augusto.
Borrowed from Latin agrum, from Proto-Italic *agros, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros.
From Latin āla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus (“white”). Compare French aube.
Borrowed from Latin album (“blank tablet”) (19th century). Doublet of album.
From Latin albus (“white”), possibly taken as a learned term (first attested 14th century), from Proto-Italic *alβos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elbʰós.
Learned borrowing from Latin almus (“nourishing; kind”), from Proto-Italic *almos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elmos, derived from the root *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”).
From Latin altus (“high”), from Proto-Italic *altos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eltós, derived from the root *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”). Cognate with English old and Welsh allt.
From Vulgar Latin *anatria, from Latin anatem, from Proto-Italic *anats, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂t- (“duck”).
From Latin anima, from animus, from Proto-Italic *anamos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁mos, a nominal derivative of *h₂enh₁- (“breathe”). Doublet of alma.
From Latin animus.
Inherited from Latin annus, from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”).
Borrowed from Latin anus.
Learned borrowing from Latin anxius.
Inherited from Latin apertus.

parole.significato: the base upon which objects were sacrificed to the gods by fire
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin āra, from Old Latin āsa, from Proto-Italic *āzā (“altar”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHsh₂- (“hearth, fireplace”), derived from the root *h₂eHs- (“to burn; hearth”).
From Latin arāre, from Proto-Italic *araō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éryeti (“to plough”), from the root *h₂erh₃-.
From Latin arcus.
From Latin arcus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo- (“bow, arrow”).

From Latin argentum, from Proto-Italic *argentom. See also the obsolete variant form ariento, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *aregentum; cf. also Old Galician-Portuguese and Old Spanish arento, Spanish arienzo.
From Latin arguere, with change of conjugation.
From Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms, weapons of war, war, defense, tools”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).

parole.significato: haruspex (one who practices divination by inspecting entrails)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin haruspicem, from Proto-Italic *haruspeks (“diviner”, literally “who examines intestines”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥H-u-, from the root *ǵʰerH- (“bowels, intestines”), plus the root *speḱ- (“to see, look, observe”).

parole.significato: to cause a sweet smell, to waft perfume
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *aulēre, diphthongized form of Latin olēre (with a later change in a conjugation), from an earlier form olō, from Proto-Italic *odō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to smell”). Doublet of olire.
Learned borrowing from Latin aurum, from earlier ausum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éh₂usom (“glow”), derived from the root *h₂ews-. Doublet of oro.
From Latin aurōra, from an ā-stem extension of Proto-Italic *auzōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwsōs.
Inherited from Latin habēre.
From Latin barba, from Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂ (“beard”).

parole.significato: nice, fair, fine, pleasant; beautiful (of the weather, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin bellus.
Inherited from Latin bene.

From a contraction of earlier bevere, from Latin bibere, from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti. Cognate with Albanian pi, literary Armenian ըմպել (əmpel), Hindi पीना (pīnā), and Irish ibh.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin bis (“twice”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin bonus, either through English or influenced by English. Compare the inherited doublet buono (“good”).

parole.significato: the coldest period of winter; winter itself
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin brūma.
Inherited from Latin bonus. Doublet of bonus, a later borrowing.
From Latin cadentem.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin form *carabriōnem, from Latin crābrōnem, from Proto-Italic *krāzrō, from a Proto-Indo-European form *krH-s-r-o, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“head”).
From Latin calēre, from Proto-Italic *kalēō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelh₁-. Compare French chaloir, Catalan caldre, caler.
From Latin calvus.
From Latin campus (“wild field”). Compare English camp.
Inherited from Latin candēre (“to shine, gleam white”), from Proto-Italic *kandēō, from Proto-Indo-European *kand- (“to shine, glow”).
Inherited from Latin cānus (“white, hoary”), from Proto-Italic *kaznos (“grey”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *ḱas-. Compare Portuguese cão.

Inherited from Latin capiō (“to take in, understand”), from Proto-Italic *kapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyéti, from the root *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Compare Galician, Spanish, and Portuguese caber (“to fit”), Catalan capir (“to understand”), and German kapieren (“to understand”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *káput. Doublet of chef.
From Latin caprīnus.
Inherited from Latin caprum.

parole.significato: a cylindrical container used chiefly to store books
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin capsa. Doublet of cassa.

From Latin carcerem, from Proto-Italic *karkros, from Proto-Indo-European *kr-kr- (“circular”), reduplication of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”), in the sense of “enclosure”. Cognate to Old Catalan càrcer/carçre, Spanish cárcel and Portuguese cárcere.
Inherited from Latin carnem (“flesh”, “meat”), from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”).
Borrowed from Latin cāsus.
Borrowed from Latin cassus (“hollow”, “empty”).

parole.significato: chaste (abstaining from immoral or unlawful sexual intercourse)
parole.testo: Uncertain if inherited or borrowed from Latin castus.
From Latin catīnus, from Proto-Italic *katinos.
From Latin cavus.
Inherited from Latin cēna, from Proto-Italic *kertsnā, from Proto-Indo-European *kért-s-nh₂ (“portion”), from *ker-, *sker-. Compare Spanish cena, Portuguese ceia and Romanian cină.
From Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.
Borrowed from Latin Cererem.
From Latin cernere, from Proto-Italic *krinō, from Proto-Indo-European *krey-.
Inherited from Latin certus.

From Latin cerebellum, derived from cerebrum, from Proto-Italic *kerazrom, from a Proto-Indo-European form *ḱerh₂-s-rom, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“head”). The alternative plural cervella derives from the Latin plural form cerebella. Doublet of the borrowing cerebello; cf. the derived cerebellare.

parole.significato: he/she/they who, those who, the ones who; (archaic) whom
parole.testo: From Latin quī, from Old Latin quei, from Proto-Italic *kʷoi.
From Latin clāvem, from Proto-Italic *klāwis, of ultimately Proto-Indo-European origin.
From Latin clīnāre (“to slope or incline; to bend; to sink”), from Proto-Italic *kl(e)inō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.
From Latin caecus, from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed”).
From Latin caelum, from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-.
Inherited from Latin cīnque.
Borrowed from Latin cīvem, from Proto-Italic *keiwis (“society”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱéy-wo-s (“intimate, friendly”), derived from the root *ḱey- (“to settle”).
Learned borrowing from Latin classis.

Learned borrowing from Latin clāvus (“nail; stripe on a tunic; callus”), from Proto-Italic *klāwos, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂wos, derived from the root *(s)kleh₂w- (“hook, crook, peg”). Doublet of chiodo, chiavo, and chiovo.
Borrowed from Latin clūnem (“buttock”), from Proto-Italic *klounis, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlównis (“buttocks, hip”).

Borrowed from Latin colere (“to worship” ← “to protect” ← “to cultivate”), from earlier *quelō, from Proto-Italic *kʷelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷéleti, derived from the root *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”).
From Latin culmen, from Proto-Italic *kolamen, from Proto-Indo-European *kelH-. Possibly influenced by cumulus or culmus phonetically. Compare Spanish colmo. Doublet of the borrowed culmine.
Inherited from Latin culpa, from Proto-Italic *kʷolpā (“wrong, mistake”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷolp-eh₂ (“bend, turn”), from *kʷelp-.

From Latin commūnem, case form of commūnis (“common, ordinary”), from Old Latin com(m)oinis, from Proto-Italic *kommoinis, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom-moy-ni-, derived from *ḱóm (“near, with”) and the root *mey- (“to exchange”).
Inherited from Latin cum (“with”), from Proto-Italic *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”).
From Latin contra (“against”).
Inherited from Latin cornū, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“horn”).

parole.significato: to run [auxiliary essere or avere] (see above)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin currere, from Proto-Italic *korzō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥s-é-ti, zero-grade thematic present of *ḱers- (“to run”).
From Latin corvus, from Proto-Italic *korwos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂wós.
Inherited from Late Latin coxa (“thigh”), from Proto-Italic *koksā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂, from *koḱs- (“joint, limb”) + *-eh₂.
Inherited from Latin coctus.

parole.significato: to brood, to incubate (an egg) (keep an egg warm) (of a bird)
parole.testo: From Latin cubō (“to lie down”), from Proto-Italic *kubāō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb-. Doublet of cubare.
Learned borrowing from Latin crēbrum (“thick, numerous, frequent”), from Proto-Italic *krēzros, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁sro-, derived from the root *ḱer- (“to grow”).

parole.significato: to grow, to increase, to expand
parole.testo: From Latin crēscere, from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”).
Borrowed from Latin crīmen.
Borrowed from Latin crīmine.

parole.significato: any hair from the mane or tail of a horse or other similar animal
parole.testo: From Latin crīnis, from Proto-Italic *kriznis, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kre-i-s-, extension of the root *(s)ker- (“to turn; to bend”).
From Latin crucem.

parole.significato: to lie; to be lying down
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cubō (“to lie down”), from Proto-Italic *kubāō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb-. Doublet of covare.

From Vulgar Latin *cunla, syncopated form of cūnula, diminutive of Latin cūna, cūnae (“cradle”), from Proto-Italic *koinā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoyneh₂, derived from the root *ḱey- (“to be lying down; to settle”). Doublet of cuna.

Inherited from Latin cūna, from Proto-Italic *koinā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoyneh₂, derived from the root *ḱey- (“to be lying down; to settle”). Doublet of culla, from a Vulgar Latin diminutive form.
Inherited from Latin corium.
Borrowed from Latin cūria.

Borrowed from Latin currus (“chariot”), from Proto-Italic *korzos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós (“vehicle”), derived from *ḱers- (“to run”). Cognate with English horse, and Welsh car (“car”). Doublet of carro.
Inherited from Latin damnum, from Proto-Italic *dapnom, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂pnóm (“expense, investment”), derived from *deh₂p- (“to sacrifice”).
Borrowed from Latin dapem (“sacrificial feast”), from Proto-Italic *daps, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂ps, derived from the root *deh₂p- (“to sacrifice; to lose”).

parole.significato: to give (to transfer the possession/holding of something to someone else)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dō, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, from the root *deh₃- (“give”).
From Latin dignus, from Proto-Italic *degnos, from Proto-Indo-European *dḱ-nós, from *deḱ- (“to take”).
From Latin Decembrem.

parole.significato: each day, a day, used in prescriptions to denote daily consumption of a drug
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin diēs, back-formed from the accusative diem (whose vowel was once long), from Proto-Italic *djēm, from Proto-Indo-European *dyew- (“heaven, sky; to shine”). Doublet of dia.
Inherited from Latin decem.
From Vulgar Latin, from Latin ieiūnus. The Latin derives from Proto-Italic *jagjūnos, itself from Proto-Indo-European *Hyeh₂ǵ-yu-, adjectival form of *Hyeh₂ǵ-ye/o- (“to sacrifice”).
From Latin deus, from earlier *dẹ̄vos, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós, derived from the root *dyew- (“sky, heaven”).

parole.significato: to utter (produce (speech or other sounds) with one's voice)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).

parole.significato: of or pertaining to a god or deity; divine
parole.testo: From Latin dīvīnus.
Borrowed from Latin dīvus.

parole.significato: to hurt, to ache (of a body part)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dolēre, from Proto-Italic *doleō (“hurt, cause pain”), from Proto-Indo-European *dolh₁éyeti (“divide”), from *delh₁- (“cut”).
Derived from Latin domāre, from Proto-Italic *domaō, from Proto-Indo-European *domh₂éyeti, causative form of the root *demh₂- (“to domesticate, tame”).
Borrowed from Latin dominus. Doublet of don.

Borrowed from Latin domitus, perfect passive participle of domō (“to tame, conquer”) originating from Proto-Italic *domatos, from Proto-Indo-European *domh₂tos, derived from the root *demh₂- (“to tame”).
Inherited from Latin dōnāre.
From Latin dōnum (“gift”).
Inherited from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.

Inherited from Latin duae ~ duas, feminine plural of duo, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Attempts at gender distinction are still found in Old Italian, but the different forms soon became interchangeable variants. The victory of due may be due to its being the phonetically

From Latin dūrus, from Proto-Italic *dūros, from Proto-Indo-European *duh₂-ró-s (“long”), from *dweh₂- (“far, long”). Cognate with Ancient Greek δηρός (dērós, “long”), Sanskrit दूर (dūrá, “distant, far, long”).
From the older form die, inherited from Latin diēs, back-formed from the accusative diem (whose vowel was once long), from Proto-Italic *djēm, from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”).
From Latin ēbrius, from Proto-Italic *ēɣʷrios, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ēgʷʰryos, derived from the root *h₁egʷʰ- (“to drink”).
Borrowed from Latin ego.

parole.significato: age (number of years in someone's life)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin aetātem.
Borrowed from Latin ēvellere (“to tear, pull or pluck out; to erase, eradicate”). Piecewise doublet of svellere.

Borrowed from Latin aevum, from earlier aevom, from Old Latin aivom, from Proto-Italic *aiwom (“period”, “age”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂óyu (“long time”, “lifetime”), from the root *h₂ey- (“vital force”, “life”, “age”, “eternity”).
From a nominalization of the Latin fāgeus, from fāgus, from Proto-Italic *fāgos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos (“beech tree”).

parole.significato: to miss, to not hit (a target, a ball, etc.)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere.
From Latin falsus, from fallere.
Borrowed from Latin famulus, from Proto-Italic *famelos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰh₁-m-eló-, derived from the root *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place”).
Inherited from Late Latin fāre.
Inherited from Latin fātum.

From fatto, from Latin factus (“done”, “made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“to do, make”), from Proto-Italic *fakiō, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place”). By surface analysis, fatto (“stoned”, “high”) + -one (augmentative suffix).
Inherited from Latin filicem.
Inherited from Latin fēmina.
From Latin findere, from Proto-Italic *findō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).
From Latin firmus, from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”).
From Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstus (“festive”).

From Latin flamma, from Proto-Italic *flāgmā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₂gmeh₂, derived from an extension of the root *bʰel- (“shiny, white”). Compare French flamme, Portuguese chama, Spanish llama.

From Latin flammeus (“flaming, fiery”), derived from flamma (“flame”), from Proto-Italic *flāgmā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₂gmeh₂, derived from an extension of the root *bʰel- (“shiny, white”). Doublet of flammeo. By surface analysis, fiamma + eo.

parole.significato: to thrust, to drive, to stick
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fīgō.
Inherited from Latin fīlum.
Inherited from Latin flōrem.
Borrowed from Latin flagrāre (“to burn, to blaze”), derived from Proto-Italic *flagros, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₂gro-, derived from an extension of the root *bʰel- (“shiny, white”).

Borrowed from Latin flammeus (“flaming, fiery”), derived from flamma (“flame”), from Proto-Italic *flāgmā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₂gmeh₂, derived from an extension of the root *bʰel- (“shiny, white”). Doublet of fiammeo.

parole.significato: sheet (rectangular piece of paper; a thin, flat layer of another material)
parole.testo: From Latin folium.
Inherited from Latin fundere, from Proto-Italic *hundō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd-.
From Latin furnus, from Proto-Italic *fornos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰr̥-nós, from *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”).
From Latin fortem
From Latin frāter, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.
From Latin frātellus, a diminutive of Latin frāter, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.
Inherited from Latin fremere.
Inherited from Latin frēnum.
From Latin frequentem.

parole.significato: to have the use, make use, to take advantage [with di ‘of something’]
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fruī.
Inherited from Latin frustum.

parole.significato: to escape, run away, scurry away
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with Sicilian fùjiri.
Borrowed from Latin fulgēre.
From Latin fūmus, from Proto-Italic *fūmos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós.
Borrowed from Latin fūr, from Proto-Italic *fōr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰṓr, derived from the root *bʰer- (“to carry”).
From Latin fūsus, past participle of fundō (“to pour out”), from Proto-Italic *hundō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd-.
From Latin gemellus, diminutive of geminus, from Proto-Italic *jemanos, from Proto-Indo-European *yemH-. Compare French jumeau, Portuguese gêmeo, Romanian geamăn, Spanish gemelo.
Borrowed from Latin generis.

From Latin germen (“seed; origin”), from Proto-Italic *genamen, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁mn̥ (“offspring, seed”), derived from the root *ǵenh₁- (“to give birth, to beget”). Cognate with Irish giniúint (“procreation, birth”).
Inherited from Latin iugum.
Borrowed from Latin iūbilāre.

parole.significato: to arrive, to reach, to come
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin iungere (“to join”), from Proto-Italic *jungō, from Proto-Indo-European *yunégti ~ *yungénti, from the root *yewg-, whence also Romanian ajunge.
From Latin iūre, form of iūs (“law”, “right”), from Proto-Italic *jowos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yéw-os, from the root *h₂yew- (“justice”, “law”).
From Latin grāna, from grānum (“grain”).

From *cranclu(m), accusative singular of Vulgar Latin *cranclus, by metathesis and syncope from a Late Latin *cancrulus (compare attested Medieval Latin cancrulus), a diminutive of Latin cancer (“crab”). The Latin derives from Proto-Italic *kankros, dissimilation of *karkros (“enclosure”) (because t
Borrowed from Latin grātus (whence also grado, an inherited doublet), from Proto-Italic *gʷrātos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥Htós, derived from the root *gʷerH- (“to praise; to elevate”).
Inherited from Latin gravis. Doublet of greve.
From Latin gustus (“taste”), from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.
Inherited from Latin heri.
From Latin imāginem (“image, imitation”), from Proto-Italic *imā (“copy”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym- (“copy”). Doublet of imago, and also the now-archaic mania.
Inherited from Latin in.
Learned borrowing from Latin inter.
Borrowed from Latin iugerum, from Proto-Italic *jougos (“team of yoked animals”), from Proto-Indo-European *yéwgos, from the root *yewg- (“to join, tie together”).
From Latin illa(m), feminine form of ille.
From Latin lāna.
Borrowed from Latin lapis. Doublet of lapide.
From Latin lēgem.
Learned borrowing from Latin līberum.
Borrowed from Latin librum (“book”).
From Latin levem (“light (not heavy)”), from Proto-Italic *leɣʷis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁léngʰus (“lightweight”), from *h₁lengʷʰ- (“light”).
From earlier lengua, from Latin lingua.
From Latin lībra.
From Latin lītem.

From Latin lumbus, possibly through Osco-Umbrian (as the expected Latin form would be *lundus), from Proto-Italic *lonðwos, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰwos, from the root *lendʰ- (“to enter, penetrate, expand”). Cognate with Old English lynd (“fat, grease”), Old English lendenu (“loins”). More at

parole.significato: light (visible electromagnetic wave; electrical device providing light)
parole.testo: From Latin lūcem (“light”), from Proto-Italic *louks, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- (“bright; white”). Doublet of the borrowed lux.
Borrowed from Latin lucrum.

From Luna, from Latin lūna, from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include Armenian լուսին (lusin), Spanish luna, Portuguese lua, Romanian lună, Russian луна́ (luná).
From the older form matre, from Latin mātrem, from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
From Latin magistrum. Doublet of mastro.
From Latin maiōrem /majjoːrɛ̃/, accusative case of maior, from Proto-Italic *magjōs, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂yós, from *méǵh₂s (“big”, “great”).
Uncertain if inherited or semi-borrowed from Latin magnus, from Proto-Italic *magnos, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂nós, derived from *méǵh₂s (“big; great”).
From Latin macrum, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós.
Inherited from Latin malus.

Inherited from Latin manus (whence also English manual, etc.), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry).
Inherited from Latin mare, from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.
Borrowed from Latin maximus.
Older form of maestro, from Latin magistrum.
From Latin māter, from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
From Latin mēta (“boundary limit”), from Proto-Italic *mētā, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”). Doublet of meta.
Inherited from Latin merda, from Proto-Italic *(s)merdā, from Proto-Indo-European *smerd-h₂- (“stench”).
Inherited from Latin mergere.
From Latin medius, whence also Italian medio (a borrowed doublet).

Inherited from Latin mīca, from Proto-Italic *smīkā, from Proto-Indo-European *smeyg- (“small, thin, delicate”). Cognate in particular with Old French mie, with whom it shares the semantic broadening from a (bread)crumb to "not (at all), few".
Borrowed from Latin milium (“millet”).
From Latin mīlle, from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂ (“one thousand”). Doublet of miglio.
Borrowed from Latin minuere.
From Old Italian meo, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.
From Latin montem.
Inherited from Latin morī(rī).
From Vulgar Latin *mortus, from Classical Latin mortuus, from Proto-Italic *mortwos, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, derived from the root *mer- (“to die; to disappear”).
Borrowed from Latin mūnus (“service, gift”), from Proto-Italic *moinos (“service”), from Proto-Indo-European *moynós, derived from the root *mey- (“to change, swap”).
Inherited from Latin nascere.
From Latin nātus, from earlier gnātus, from Proto-Italic *gnātos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁tós (“begotten, produced”), derived from the root *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, give birth”).
From Latin nāvem, from Proto-Italic *naus ~ *nāwis, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us, derived from the root *(s)neh₂- (“to swim, float”).
Borrowed from Latin nātiōnem.
Inherited from Latin nivem, from Proto-Italic *sniks, from Proto-Indo-European *snígʷʰs. Compare Portuguese neve, Spanish nieve.
Inherited from Latin nīdus, from Proto-Italic *nizdos (“nest”), from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (“nest”). Compare French nid, Spanish nido, Portuguese ninho.
From Latin nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Compare French neveu, Romanian nepot, Catalan and Occitan nebot, Sicilian niputi and Persian نوه.
From Latin nōs, from Proto-Italic *nōs.
From Latin nōmen.
From Latin nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.
Inherited from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
Inherited from Latin novembrem.

Borrowed from Late Latin novīcius, novītius derived from Latin novus, from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, from the root *new-. By surface analysis, nov- (“new”, fossilized stem for nuovo) + -izio.
Borrowed from Latin nū̆cleus (“kernel, core”).
Borrowed from Latin numerus, whence also Italian novero (an inherited doublet).
Inherited from Latin novus, from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, from the root *new-.

parole.significato: smell, odour, odor, aroma, fragrance, scent
parole.testo: From Latin odōrem, from an archaic form odōs, from Proto-Italic *odōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃édos, derived from the root *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”). Doublet of aulore and olore.
From Latin olēre (with a later change in a conjugation), from an earlier form olō, from Proto-Italic *odō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to smell”). Doublet of aulire.
Inherited from Latin opera.
Borrowed from Latin oppidum (“town”).
From Latin aurum, from earlier ausum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éh₂usom (“glow”), derived from the root *h₂ews-.
From Latin horrēre (“to dread ← to tremble, shiver ← to stand erect, stand on end”), from Proto-Italic *horzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥séh₁(ye)ti, derived from the root *ǵʰers- (“stiff”).
From Latin horrōrem, from Proto-Italic *horzōs, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰórsōs, derived from the root *ǵʰers- (“stiff; surprised”).
Inherited from Latin ursus.

From Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Compare Catalan, French, and Romanian os; Portuguese osso; Corsican, Sardinian, and Sicilian ossu; Spanish hueso.

parole.significato: army or host, especially that of the enemy
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin hostem (“enemy, stranger”), from Proto-Italic *hostis, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“guest, stranger”).
Inherited from Latin austrum. Cognate to English auster.
From Latin octō.
From Latin Octōbrem.
Derived from Old Italian patre, from Latin patrem, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.
Learned borrowing from Latin pāgus (“district”).
From Latin pālus, from Proto-Italic *pākslos, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-slos, from *peh₂ǵ-.
From Latin parentem.

parole.significato: to look, to seem, to appear
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pārēre, from Proto-Italic *pāzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).
Inherited from Latin partem, from Proto-Italic *partim.
From Latin pāscere, from Proto-Italic *pāskō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect, to shepherd”).
From Latin pater, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.
Inherited from Latin peccāre.
Inherited from Latin pecora, neuter plural of pecus (“cattle”), from pecū, from Proto-Indo-European *peḱu- (“livestock, domestic animals”).
From Latin pēdere, from Proto-Italic *pezdō, from Proto-Indo-European *pésdeti, thematic root present derived from the root *pesd- (“to fart softly”).

From Late Latin pendĕre (conjugation confused with or altered by pendere (“to suspend, hang”)) for Latin pendēre (“to hang down, to be suspended”), from Proto-Italic *pendēō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull; to spin”).
Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.
From Latin penna and pinna, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”).
From Latin per, taking many roles from Latin pro.

parole.significato: to weigh (to measure the weight of)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pēnsāre (“weigh, hang”), whence also the doublet pensare (“to think”). Compare French peser.
Inherited from Latin pectinem.
Inherited from Latin pectus, from Proto-Italic *pektos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peg- (“breast”). Compare Catalan pit, Portuguese peito, Romanian piept, Spanish pecho.

Learned borrowing from Classical Latin piāculum (“propitiatory sacrifice, atonement”), from Proto-Italic *pīāklom (“sacrifice for expiatory purposes”), derived from *pīāō (“to expiate; to propitiate”), derived from *pīos (“pious, devout”), from Proto-Indo-European *puHyós, from *pewH- (“to be clean,

From Latin plāga (hence English plague), from Proto-Italic *plāgā, from Proto-Indo-European *pl(e)h₂géh₂, derived from *pleh₂g-, an extension of the root *pel- (“to beat, push, drive”). Cognate with French plaie, Spanish llaga, Catalan plaga, Galician and Portuguese chaga, Romanian plagă, and more d
Inherited from Latin plānus. Compare Sicilian chianu.
Inherited from Latin plānum, derived from plānus.
From Latin planta, from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).

Inherited from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Compare Catalan ple, French plein, Portuguese cheio, Romanian plin, Sardinian prenu, Sicilian chinu, Spanish lleno.
Inherited from Latin pius.
Inherited from Latin plūma.
From Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ukos, derived from the root *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare French peu, Portuguese pouco, Spanish poco.
Learned borrowing from Latin pōculum, pōclum from Proto-Italic *pōtlom, from Proto-Indo-European *péh₃tlom, derived from the root *peh₃- (“to drink”). Cognate with Hindi पात्र (pātra) and Irish ól.
Inherited from Latin pōmum (“fruit”), from pōmus, from Proto-Italic *poomos, probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₂po-h₁ém-os (“taken off”), from *h₂epo (“off”) + *h₁em- (“take”).
From Latin porca (“sow”).
From Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos.
From Latin portus, from Proto-Italic *portus, from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”), from the root *per- (“to go forth”, “to cross”).

Inherited from Latin posita, feminine singular of positus, past participle of pōnō (“to put”). Originally, "post for horses or for mooring ships", then "stopping place for coaches on a journey, way station". Doublet of posta (feminine past participle of porre).
From Latin postus, from positus.
From Latin potentem.

Borrowed from Latin pōtus, from Proto-Italic *pōtos, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₃tós (“(having been) drunk; having drunk”), derived from the root *peh₃- (“to drink”). Cognate with Greek ποτό (potó, “drink, beverage”).
From Latin pretium, whence also Italian pregio, a doublet. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *préti (“back”).
From Latin prīmus, from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos.
Borrowed from Latin prior.
From Latin prīscus, from earlier *priuscus, derived from prior (“former”, “previous”), from Proto-Italic *priōs, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *per (“to go over”).

parole.significato: having strong moral principles; honest, decent, virtuous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin probus.

parole.significato: one's, one's own, her (own), its (own), their (own)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin proprius.
From Latin pugnus, from Proto-Italic *pugnos, from Proto-Indo-European *puǵnos, from *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
Inherited from Latin pungere, from Proto-Italic *pungō, from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”). Cognate with French poindre, Romanian împunge.
From Latin punctum.
Derived from Latin quattuor.
Inherited from Latin quālem.

parole.significato: how much, how many, however much, however many
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin quantus.
From Latin quattuor, from Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
Borrowed from Latin quiētem (“rest, quiet”), from Proto-Italic *kʷiētis, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyéh₁tis, from the root *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).
Inherited from Latin rādīcem.
Inherited from Latin rāmus, from Proto-Italic *wrād-mo-, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).
From Vulgar Latin *rapīre, from Latin rapere, from Proto-Italic *rapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rp-i-, from *h₁rep- (“to snatch”).
Inherited from Latin rēx, via the nominative singular, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“ruler, king”). Doublet of rege, which was borrowed from Latin via the accusative rēgem.

Learned borrowing from Latin reditūrus (“about to return”), future active participle of redeō (“to go, come back”), derived from eō (“to go”), from Proto-Italic *eō, from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₁ey- (“to go”).
Learned borrowing from Latin rēgem, from Proto-Italic *rēks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“ruler”, “king”). Doublet of re, which was inherited from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin rius (“river”), from Latin rīvus (“a small stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rih₂wós, from *h₃reyh₂- (“to flow; to move or set in motion”) and *-wós. Doublet of rivo.
Borrowed from Latin rogus, from Proto-Italic *rogos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-.
From Latin rubus, from Proto-Italic *wruðos, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰo- (“sweetbriar”).
From Latin ruber, from Proto-Italic *ruðros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rudʰrós (“red”), from the root *h₁rewdʰ-.
From Latin rota
From Latin rūsticus, derived from Proto-Italic *rowos (“country, countryside”).
Inherited from Latin sacrum, from Proto-Italic *sakros, from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂krós, derived from the root *seh₂k- (“to sanctify, to make a treaty”).
From Latin sacrātus.
Inherited from Latin salem.
Borrowed from Latin salūbrem.
From Latin sancīre (“to make sacred”), from Proto-Italic *sankjō, from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂nékti ~ *sh₂nkénti, derived from the root *seh₂k- (“sacred”).
From Classical Latin saxum, from Proto-Italic *saksom, of unknown origin. Compare Portuguese seixo (“pebble”) and Spanish saxo (“stone”).
Inherited from Latin scāla (“stair, staircase, ladder”).

Inherited from Latin scamnum, from Proto-Italic *skaβnom, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ-no-m, from *skabʰ- (“to hold up”). Cognate with Spanish escaño, Galician and Portuguese escano, Romanian scaun, Sanskrit स्कम्भ (skambhá).
From Latin scindere, from Proto-Italic *skindō, from Proto-Indo-European *skinédti (“to be cutting off”), derived from the root *skeyd- (“to split”).
Inherited from Latin scōpa.
Inherited from Latin scrībere.
Borrowed from Latin saeculum.
From Latin sedēre, from Proto-Italic *sedēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
From earlier *sequire, from Vulgar Latin *sequīre of deponent Classical Latin sequī, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sékʷetor, derived from the root *sekʷ- (“follow”).
From Latin sella, from Proto-Italic *sedlā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
Inherited from Latin sentīre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *serpes, from Latin serpēns, from serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-.

parole.significato: to snake (to follow or move in a winding route)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serpere (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-Italic *serpō, from Proto-Indo-European *sérp-e-ti ~ *sérp-onti, thematic root present of *serp- (“to creep, crawl”). Cognate with Greek έρπω (érpo, “to crawl, creep”).
From Latin servīre.
From Latin sēta, from saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese seda.
From Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
Learned borrowing from Latin sincērus (“pure, genuine”).
Inherited from Latin sinister.
Learned borrowing from Latin sinister. Doublet of sinestro.
From Latin somnium (“dream”), derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.

Inherited from Latin soldus, syncopic form of (nummus) solidus (“solid (coin)”) (referring to the gold content), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole”). Doublet of solido and sodo, and likely also saldo.

parole.significato: the state of being asleep; sleep, slumber
parole.testo: From Latin somnus, from Proto-Italic *swepnos, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos, from the root *swep- (“to sleep”). Cognate with Dalmatian samno, French somme, Lithuanian sãpnas, Romanian somn, Spanish sueño.
Learned borrowing from Latin sopōrem (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepōs, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *swep- (“to sleep”).
From Latin soror, from a diminutive form or based on the model of fratello. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *swezōr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
From Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from the Proto-Indo-European root *ser- (“to sort, lineup”).
Inherited from Latin subtus, which is derived from Latin sub. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo. Cognate to French sous.
From Latin spīca.
From Latin spīna, from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp point”).
Inherited from Latin spīnus.
Inherited from Latin stēlla, from Proto-Italic *stērlā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr. Doublet of étoile.
From Latin studeō, or through studio, from Latin studium. By surface analysis, studio + -are. Compare Spanish estudiar.
Inherited from Latin sūgere.
From Latin suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé.
Borrowed from Latin tābes (“melting, putrefaction”), derived from Proto-Italic *tāfē-, from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂bʰeh₁- (“to be melting”), derived from the root *teh₂- (“to melt; to flow”).

parole.significato: to be silent, to keep quiet
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin tacēre, from Proto-Italic *takēō, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *tak- or *tHk-.
Inherited from Latin tangere, from Proto-Italic *tangō, nasal infix present from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g-.
Inherited from Latin tardus.

parole.significato: governess (or any young woman looking after children)
parole.testo: From Latin tata.
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin taurus, from Proto-Italic *tauros, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros. Doublet of toro, which is inherited.
From Latin tendere (“to stretch, stretch out, distend, extend”), from Proto-Italic *tendō, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).
Inherited from Latin tenēre, from Proto-Italic *tenēō, stative from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).
Inherited from Latin terra, from Proto-Italic *terzā, from Proto-Indo-European *ters-eh₂, from *ters- (“dry”).
From Latin terrēnus.
From Latin tertius.
Inherited from Latin tinctus.
From earlier tollere, from Latin tollō (“to lift, remove”), from Proto-Italic *tolnō, from the Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“to bear, endure”).
With a change in conjugation, from Latin tondēre (“to shave, shear”), from Proto-Italic *tondeō, from Proto-Indo-European *tond-éye-ti, causative derivation of the root *tend- (“to split, cut off”).

Borrowed from Latin torrentem, accusative form of torrēns (“rushing”, “torrential”) (originally “scorching", then "powerful", "strengthful", "forceful"), present active participle of torreō (“to scorch, burn, parch”), from Proto-Italic *torzeō, causative of the Proto-Indo-European root *ters- (“dry”

parole.significato: torrential, torrent-like, irregular (of a river flow)
parole.testo: From torrente, from Latin torrentem, present active participle of torreō (“to scorch, burn, parch”), from Proto-Italic *torzeō, causative of the Proto-Indo-European root *ters- (“dry”). By surface analysis, torrent(e) (“torrent”, “stream”) + -izio (derivational suffix).

parole.significato: cough (condition that causes one to cough)
parole.testo: From Latin tussem, from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s- (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).
Borrowed from Latin tranquillus (“quiet, calm, still, tranquil”), from Proto-Italic *trānskʷīlos.
Inherited from Latin trabem.
Inherited from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Sicilian tri.
Borrowed from Latin tribus.
From Latin trēs, influenced by duo.
Borrowed from Latin triplus.
Inherited from Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.

From Latin tuus, from Proto-Italic *towos. In the singular, Latin tuum underwent *ʊu > *ou > *ɔu dissimilation, cf. Sardinian tou, and also Latin ōvum > Italian òvo, Spanish huevo, ultimately producing [ˈtwɔu], and a plural [ˈtwɔi]. Italian then underwent its regular *wɔV > *uV sound change, cf. *bw
From Latin ūber (“teat, udder”), from Proto-Italic *ouðer, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥.

From Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”), from Proto-Italic *awis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis. Doublet of augello, which was borrowed from Occitan. Compare Neapolitan auciello, Ligurian öxéllo, Sicilian auceḍḍu.
Borrowed from Latin ultimus.
Inherited from Latin ungere, from earlier unguō, from Proto-Italic *ongʷō, from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₃engʷ- (“to smear”, “to anoint”).
Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.
Inherited from Latin homō (nominative). The plural reflects Latin hominēs.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Latin ōvum n.
Inherited from Latin ūsus (“use, employment”), from Proto-Italic *oissos.
Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna. Doublet of guaina.
Borrowed from Latin vagus.
Inherited from Latin valēre.

parole.significato: the wooden fence built at the top of a rampart
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vallum.
Inherited from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *weyd-.
Inherited from Latin vidua, possibly through a Vulgar Latin *viduva.
From Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.

Learned borrowing from Latin vellere (“to pluck out; to depilate; to pull or tear down”), from Proto-Italic *welnō, from Proto-Indo-European *wl̥néh₃ti, derived from the root *welh₃- (“to hit, to strike”).
Inherited from Latin venīre.
From Late Latin vĭnti, from Latin vīgintī, from Proto-Italic *wīgentī, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wih₁ḱm̥ti, *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti.

parole.significato: wind (movement of air caused by differences in atmospheric pressure)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ventus (“wind”), from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts, from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

parole.significato: beauty with a specific component of gracefulness, esp. said of feminine beauty
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin venustātem (“loveliness”, “beauty”), from Proto-Italic *wenostāts (“beauty”), from Proto-Indo-European *wénh₁osteh₂ts, ultimately from the root *wenh₁- (“to love”).
From Latin verbum (“word, verb”), from Proto-Italic *werðom (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”), from root *werh₁- (“to speak, to say”) + extension *-dʰ-.
Borrowed from Latin vergere (“to turn, incline”), from Proto-Italic *wergō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wérg-e-ti, derived from the root *h₂werg- (“to turn”).
From Latin vermem, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.
Inherited from Latin vērus (“true”), from Proto-Italic *wēros, from a Proto-Indo-European *weh₁-ros, from *weh₁- (“true”).
Inherited from Latin vestem.
From Latin vitrum, from Proto-Italic *wedrom, from Proto-Indo-European *wedro- (“water-like”), derived from the root *wed- (“water”). Cognate with French verre, Portuguese vidro, Spanish vidrio.
From Latin via.
From Latin vetus (“old”), from Proto-Italic *wetos (“year”), from Proto-Indo-European *wétos.
Inherited from Latin vigilem.
Inherited from Latin vincere, from Proto-Italic *winkō, from Proto-Indo-European *wi-n-k-, from *weyk- (“to overcome”) with a nasal infix.

parole.significato: wine (an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting grape juice, with an ABV ranging from 5.5–16%)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wéyh₁nom, derived from *wéyh₁ō (“vine, wine”). Cognates include Albanian verë, Armenian գինի (gini) and Greek οίνος (oínos).
Borrowed from Latin vīrus.

parole.significato: viewer; apparatus for viewing (slides, microfilm, etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin vīsōrem (“viewer, watcher”) from videō (“to view, watch”), from Proto-Italic *widēō (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see”).
From Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā, possibly a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wo-teh₂, from the root *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”).
From Latin vītem
From Latin vīvere, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (“to live, be alive”).
From Latin vīvus (“alive”, “living”), from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).
Inherited from Latin vōx, vōcem.
From Latin vōs, from Old Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs, ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs. Cognates with the same usage are the French vous and the Russian вы (vy).
Inherited from Latin volāre, from Proto-Italic *gʷelāō.
Inherited from Latin vulpēs (accusative vulpem) from earlier volpēs, from Proto-Italic *wolpis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl(o)p ~ *h₂ulp (“(red) fox”).
Inherited from Latin vostrum, which is the accusative of voster, which derives from the older form vester, from Proto-Italic *westeros.
From Latin vōtum.
